definition: In Hustler Magazine, Inc. v. Falwell, 485 U.S. 46 (1988), the Supreme Court held that the First Amendment free speech protections, along with the incorporation doctrine of the Fourteenth Amendment bar public figures from recovering damages for intentional infliction of emotional distress (IIED) arising from a publication, unless they can prove that the publication contained a false statement of fact made with actual malice. Overview Jerry Falwell, a public figure and well-known televangelist, sued Hustler Magazine for libel, invasion of privacy, and IIED after the magazine published a parody advertisement suggesting immoral behavior. The ad included a disclaimer labeling it as parody and “not to be taken seriously.” The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Virginia entered a directed verdict for Hustler Magazine on the invasion of privacy claim. The jury found for the defendant on the libel claim but awarded Falwell damages for IIED. The Fourth Circuit affirmed the judgment, rejecting the argument that the New York Times Co. v. Sullivan, 376 U.S. 254 (1964), “actual malice” standard should apply to IIED claims. Hustler Magazine appealed to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court reversed. Chief Justice Rehnquist, writing for a unanimous Court, held that the constitutional protections of free expression extend to speech that causes emotional distress to public figures when that speech cannot reasonably be interpreted as stating actual facts. The Court reasoned that allowing recovery based solely on “outrageousness” would enable juries to punish unpopular or offensive speech in violation of the First Amendment. The Court’s reference to the Fourteenth Amendment reflects the doctrine of incorporation, which applies the protections of the First Amendment to the states. Because Falwell’s claim arose under state tort law, the Court relied on the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause to ensure that state courts could not impose liability inconsistent with federal constitutional standards. The First Amendment’s free speech protections, incorporated through the Fourteenth Amendment, limited Virginia’s ability to impose IIED liability on Hustler Magazine.
